source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2006) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R
finding: ACT-R scores each production as U = P*G - C (chance of reaching the goal times goal value, minus cost in time). Choice among matching productions is a noisy softmax. Both P and C are learned from experience, G is a fixed parameter.
numbers: Formula U_i = P_i G - C_i; P(i) = e^(U_i/t) / sum_j e^(U_j/t). P = successes/(successes+failures). Noise t is a free parameter.
quote: Utility learning ... ACT-R will tend to select the strategy with the highest utility.
limits: A chapter by the architecture authors, not an independent test. The text says the best-utility strategy is chosen but others are sampled at a rate set by noise.
agent_relevance: This is the exact rule behind 'choose an operator by success rate': keep success and cost counts per operator, add noise so weak operators still get sampled.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2006) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R (reports Lovett's Building Sticks Task data)
finding: In the Building Sticks Task people first follow a hill-climbing bias (pick the stick that looks closest to the goal), then shift to whichever strategy (overshoot or undershoot) has actually worked. A 4-rule utility model fits the shift. Rule 4 'undershoot if middle stick is closer' lost utility by problem 7 so 'always overshoot' won.
numbers: 15 problems. Both strategies work on problems 1 and 15; only overshoot on 2-8 and 12-14; only undershoot on 9-11. Over 80% chose overshoot on problem 5 (where hill-climbing also favoured it). People adapted almost immediately at problem 9 when overshoot stopped working.
limits: Chapter gives a figure and prose from one of Lovett's experiments; sample size and fit statistics are not given in the chapter. The model started with a built-in prior for hill-climbing rules.
agent_relevance: Shows history-of-success beats surface cues after a few trials, and that a prior bias can be overridden. Our agent should let operator success counts overturn its default heuristic quickly and re-adapt when a regime flips.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2006) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R (Sugar Factory model)
finding: An ACT-R model of the Sugar Factory control task (Berry and Broadbent) learns from stored instances, not rule utilities, and matches how many on-target decisions people make.
numbers: On-target decisions out of 40 trials: people 8 in block 1 and 15 in block 2; model 9 and 14.
limits: Only two blocks of group means. A good fit does not show that instances rather than utilities are the mechanism.
agent_relevance: Boundary: not every skill gain is utility learning. Some is instance memory. A scaffold should keep both a success tally for operators and a memory of past cases.

source: Lebiere, Wallach & Taatgen (1998) ACT-R Symposium: implicit and explicit learning
finding: Competing explanations for Sugar Factory learning: the Dienes and Fahey instance race model versus an ACT-R model that keeps all instances and uses production rules for prior algorithmic knowledge. The rival model needed extra assumptions that people could not know.
numbers: Dienes and Fahey saw that 86% of the first ten inputs were explained by three simple rules. Their model stored only 'successful' instances using a loose target of 9000 tons +/-1000 that participants were not told. When they stored all instances the fit got worse; the ACT-R model stores every instance and has no free parameter for the count of prior instances.
limits: Symposium paper. Numeric fit scores are in figures, not text.
agent_relevance: Warns that credit by success can leak outcome knowledge. If our agent keeps only wins in memory it gets a cleaner but less realistic view; keep failures too.

source: Brasoveanu & Dotlacil (2020) Reinforcement learning for production-based cognitive models - 1-stimulus lexical decision
finding: Treat ACT-R rules as RL actions and let tabular Q-learning learn when each rule fires, with goal-state conditions removed. For the shortest task it learns the rule order perfectly.
numbers: 15,000 episodes simulated. After about 5,000 episodes the task finishes in the ideal 12 steps. 8 states with non-zero Q values, all correct. Settings: learning rate 1e-3, discount 0.95, epsilon annealed from 1 to 0.01 (times 1-1e-5 per step), rule firing 50 ms.
limits: Toy task, 4 rules, tabular. Not compared to humans.
agent_relevance: Evidence that rule selection by learned value can recover a hand-coded control flow, but only in a tiny space.

source: Brasoveanu & Dotlacil (2020) Reinforcement learning for production-based cognitive models - 2-stimuli task
finding: With one word and one non-word the agent needs more trials and is slightly imperfect.
numbers: 15,000 episodes; about 9,000 to reach the ideal 18 steps. 13 states with non-zero values; one state-action pair stays wrong (fires 'retrieving' when it should not).
limits: Same toy limits.
agent_relevance: Learning cost grows quickly with task length even in a four-rule world.

source: Brasoveanu & Dotlacil (2020) Reinforcement learning for production-based cognitive models - 4-stimuli task and failure at length
finding: With four stimuli the agent is still noisy after 25,000 episodes. The authors say credit assignment over long sparse-reward tasks is the main problem, and pilot parsing models were much harder.
numbers: 25,000 episodes; about 22,000 to finish reliably in under 40 steps (ideal is 34). 24 states with non-zero values: 18 correct, 6 nonsensical. Agent still sometimes waits (None action) for no reason.
quote: standard RL methods are increasingly ineffective in this kind of sparse-reward, long time horizon tasks
limits: Failure to scale is stated in the paper; no deep-RL result is reported.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for 'choose by success rate': with many steps and one end reward, plain value learning is slow. Our agent should score operators at step level with intermediate checks.

source: Brasoveanu & Dotlacil (2020) Reinforcement learning for production-based cognitive models - reward design
finding: The learned policy depends on the reward shape: +1 at the goal, -0.15 per rule fired, and a negative reward equal to elapsed time. Without a time penalty the agent can stall by selecting 'do nothing' until a 2 second timeout.
numbers: Reward +1 at goal; -0.15 per intermediate firing; none for waiting; time penalty = seconds elapsed. Max wait 2 s per word.
limits: Reward constants were chosen by the authors; no sensitivity sweep shown.
agent_relevance: Cost must be part of utility (as in U = PG - C), otherwise the policy idles or loops. Tell the agent what a step costs.

source: Gall & Fruehwirth (2014) Exchanging conflict resolution in an adaptable implementation of ACT-R
finding: An independent re-implementation of ACT-R in Constraint Handling Rules reproduced the reference Lisp results for reinforcement-based utility learning exactly (when rounded) on a rock-paper-scissors model, and for the older success/cost rule too. It also built the first implementation of 'random estimated costs'.
numbers: Rock-paper-scissors, 20 samples of 20 moves per opponent, 2 s simulated time per sample, noise off. Always-rock opponent: average final utilities (rock, paper, scissors) = (0, 1.87, -0.02). Rock-or-paper opponent: (0, 0.81, 0.49). Random opponent: 6.6 wins, 6.7 draws, 6.7 defeats, so chance. Random-cost strategy used 3 samples x 50 runs.
limits: Noise was switched off, so stochastic selection was not tested. Tiny model with no declarative or perceptual modules.
agent_relevance: Utility learning is easy to specify and reproduces cleanly. It finds the exploit against a biased opponent and stays at chance against a random one, which is the right behaviour.

source: Gall & Fruehwirth (2014) Exchanging conflict resolution in an adaptable implementation of ACT-R - reproducibility problems
finding: The reference implementations differ on details that theory leaves open. When two productions have equal utility the winner is undocumented and differs between ACT-R 5.0 and 6.0. The RL utility rule exists only in 6.0; the success/cost rule only ran in 5.0.
numbers: One sample (75% paper in the first 9 moves) made scissors the top utility (Us=1.329 vs Up=0), still 15 wins, 5 defeats, 0 draws. The success/cost rule failed to find the best move against the always-rock opponent because of rule order.
limits: Authors say noise would hide tie-break differences in normal use.
agent_relevance: Ties and rule order change outcomes. Our selector should break ties on purpose (for example cheaper operator first) and log it.

source: Gray, Sims, Fu & Schoelles (2006) The soft constraints hypothesis - three experiments
finding: People choose between looking again (interaction-intensive) and remembering (memory-intensive) by time cost-benefit, as ACT-R utility predicts. As the cost of looking rose, they looked less and placed more blocks from memory. This runs against the 'minimum memory' idea that people always save memory.
numbers: 3 experiments, 16 to 18 participants per between-subjects condition (undergraduates). Exp 3 used six lockout times from 0 to 3,200 ms. Target-window accesses: linear trend over lockout accounted for 98% of condition variance; another measure 87%. Exp 1: low vs high and med vs high differed (p<.0008, p<.0039) but low vs med (46 ms difference) did not.
limits: Lab task (Blocks World copy task), one cost currency (time); differences below about 50 ms not detected. Only undergraduates.
agent_relevance: Operator choice follows expected time cost even at the sub-second level. Include cost in the operator score, not only success.

source: Gray, Sims, Fu & Schoelles (2006) The soft constraints hypothesis - effect sizes in Exp 1
finding: In Exp 1 the high-cost group looked longer on first look and placed more blocks per look, meaning they shifted toward a memory-heavy method.
numbers: Duration of first look: 1179, 1241 and 2334 ms for low, medium and high cost conditions (column order as printed). Blocks placed after first look: 1.7, 1.9 and 2.9.
limits: Column order read from extracted text; check against Table 1 before quoting.
agent_relevance: Concrete size of the cost-driven strategy shift, useful for calibrating the weight on cost.

source: Gray, Sims, Fu & Schoelles (2006) The soft constraints hypothesis - Ideal Performer Model
finding: A Q-learning 'ideal performer' using ACT-R memory equations picked the time-minimizing strategy per lockout condition, then a softmax converted utilities to choice with fitted noise. Model and data agreed that people trade off by time.
numbers: Fitted noise t = 0.491 by least-squares; with a 1 s difference in expected time the model picks the faster strategy 88.5% of the time. Eight ENCODE-k strategies for 8 blocks.
limits: Parameters (retrieval threshold, latency, noise) were fit to the same data, so the fit is not out-of-sample.
agent_relevance: With modest noise, choice among operators is near-greedy for a 1 s gap and mixed for tiny gaps. Pick the noise level explicitly.

source: Fu & Anderson (2006) From recurrent choice to skill learning: a reinforcement-learning model
finding: Search result shows the paper extends ACT-R utility learning as a temporal-difference reinforcement-learning rule and says it explains violations of independence, preference reversals and the goal gradient in maze learning.
numbers: Not read this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Full text not obtained (ACT-R site unreachable). Treat as pointer only.
agent_relevance: Source of the TD form U(n) = U(n-1) + a[R(n) - U(n-1)] used by ACT-R 6 and by LLM-ACTR.

source: Brasoveanu & Dotlacil (2021) Production-system RL vs ACT-R utility learning (Topics in Cognitive Science)
finding: Search snippet says they compare tabular Q-learning and deep Q-networks with ACT-R utility learning as baseline for production selection.
numbers: Not read this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Follow-up if we want a deep-RL versus utility-learning comparison.

source: Wu, Oltramari, Francis, Giles & Ritter (2024) Cognitive LLMs (LLM-ACTR) - hold-out accuracy
finding: A Llama-2 13B model fine-tuned on traces of an ACT-R model (VSM-ACTR, manufacturing decision task) predicted the ACT-R model's choices better than chance and much better than un-tuned Llama.
numbers: Hold-out: chance accuracy 0.4826 (NLL 0.6931); un-tuned Llama accuracy 0.3564 (NLL 1.1330); LLM-ACTR accuracy 0.6576 (NLL 0.6534). 2,012 trials, 32 problem sets, 15-16 trials per run, 10-fold CV.
limits: Target is a simulated ACT-R agent, not people. The claimed gain over chain-of-thought baselines is not in the results table; baselines are chance and plain Llama only.
agent_relevance: LLMs imitate utility-based choice only after tuning. Un-tuned Llama was below chance, so do not expect prompting alone to reproduce utility-driven operator choice.

source: Wu, Oltramari, Francis, Giles & Ritter (2024) Cognitive LLMs (LLM-ACTR) - single versus multi-facet
finding: Accuracy fell when the target included both the choice and the strategy level (novice, intermediate, expert).
numbers: Single-facet: accuracy 0.64, NLL 0.63. Multi-facet (6 classes): accuracy 0.42, NLL 1.18.
limits: Six-class chance is about 0.17 so 0.42 is still above chance; the authors do not state this.
agent_relevance: Strategy level is harder to read out of an LLM than the binary choice.

source: Wu, Oltramari, Francis, Giles & Ritter (2024) Cognitive LLMs (LLM-ACTR) - learning trajectory and null result
finding: The ACT-R model with TD utility updates (alpha 0.2) moves from novice to expert strategies with trials. Adding the full ACT-R reasoning-trace embeddings to the LLM embedding gave no gain.
numbers: Trials coefficient 0.086 (P<0.05); random-group variance 0.007. Ordered logistic thresholds: novice to intermediate 0.88 (P<0.05), intermediate to expert 0.1 (P=0.021). Concatenating 240 full-trace embeddings: no significant improvement, accuracy 0.71 for both datasets.
limits: Statistics describe simulated data. Paper reports a ragged-tensor problem in the full-trace route.
agent_relevance: Learning curve of utility-based selection is steep early and flatter later. Trace injection did not help in this test.

source: Wu, Oltramari, Francis, Giles & Ritter (2024) Cognitive LLMs (LLM-ACTR) - example penalty update
finding: Worked example of a utility update with a penalty: reward -2 minus 0.5 time step gives -2.5, and the novice strategy utility goes from U(6) to U(7) = -1.02 with alpha 0.2.
numbers: U(n) = U(n-1) + 0.2[R(n) + U(n-1)] as printed in the paper; result -1.02.
limits: The printed equation has a plus sign before U(n-1) where standard TD has a minus. Treat the sign as unverified.
agent_relevance: Shows the update scale: one bad outcome moves utility by about a fifth of the error.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang & Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context? - main result
finding: Out of all tested prompt designs on GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2 in multi-armed bandits, only one configuration explored well: GPT-4 with chain-of-thought and externally summarized history (counts and means). The rest behaved like greedy.
numbers: 32 prompt designs, about 50K GPT-4 queries; main runs T=100 rounds, gap 0.2, K=5 arms, N=10 or 20 replicates. Success config: summarized history, suggestive framing, chain-of-thought, T=200, N=40, reward comparable to Thompson Sampling.
limits: Authors say N and T are too small for reward-based significance, so they use surrogate statistics. Only Bernoulli bandits.
agent_relevance: Direct test of 'pick the operator by success rate'. Raw logs do not work; a pre-computed table of successes and tries per operator does. The scaffold must supply the tally.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang & Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context? - failure mode
finding: With the basic prompt, GPT-4 at temperature 0 mostly locks onto one arm early (suffix failure).
numbers: T=500, N=20: more than 60% of replicates chose the best arm only a handful of times and never recovered, like Greedy.
limits: One prompt, one model family at the time.
agent_relevance: Without forced exploration an LLM will exploit the first good-looking operator. Add an exploration rule (try each operator at least k times).

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 - bandit and horizon task
finding: GPT-3 (davinci) did well on bandit tasks but did not show human-like directed exploration. On the horizon task its overall regret was lower than humans.
numbers: Horizon task: overall regret GPT-3 M=2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans M=3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878)=-5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: indistinguishable from humans, t(5566)=-0.043, p=.97. Descriptions task (13,000 problems): davinci below human level, t(29134)=-11.50, p<.001.
limits: GPT-3 only, text prompts, human data from another study. Newer models not tested.
agent_relevance: Even a small LLM can pick on payoff, but exploring for information needs to be scaffolded.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 - vignettes
finding: GPT-3 gave the correct or a human-like wrong answer on all standard vignettes but made non-human mistakes on adversarial rewordings.
numbers: 12 of 12 standard vignettes correct or human-like; adversarial versions produced non-human-like errors. Behaviour depended on presentation.
limits: Training-set contamination is possible.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording changes operator choice, so keep operator descriptions fixed and score by outcomes.

source: Nie, Su, Chang et al. (2024) EVOLvE: Evaluating and optimizing LLMs for exploration - inference-time support
finding: Giving the LLM summaries or UCB-style numbers helps. Win-rate against baselines rose from raw history to summarized history to algorithm-guided support for the larger models.
numbers: MAB win-rate %: Raw history: Gemma-2B 7.6, Gemma-9B 10.5, Gemini Flash 27.7, Pro 45.5. Summarized: 10.5, 5.3, 34.8, 60.0. Algorithm-guided: 4.9, 4.1, 32.2, 59.6. UCB itself 90.6. Contextual bandit: Flash 0.0 raw vs 46.4 guided; Pro 7.1 vs 64.3; LinUCB 96.4.
limits: Small models got worse with guidance. Google models, synthetic bandits.
agent_relevance: Success tallies plus a confidence bonus help big models but not tiny ones. Do not over-structure for weak backbones.

source: Nie, Su, Chang et al. (2024) EVOLvE: Evaluating and optimizing LLMs for exploration - distillation and exploration traces
finding: Fine-tuning on UCB trajectories beat few-shot. Few-shot hurt Pro in some setups. Without help Flash barely explored.
numbers: Oracle fine-tuned Flash MAB win-rate 65.6 (hard-task data) vs 54.5 (easy-task data); few-shot Flash 50.2 (easy demos) vs 43.0 (hard demos); few-shot Pro with algorithm support 56.4 vs raw-history 39.1. Optimal-arm fraction: UCB 32.7% to 65.0%, Flash 9.3% to 10.7%. Least-tried-arm fraction: UCB 82.3% to 15.3%, Flash 11.3% to 1.1%.
limits: Fine-tuning is not available to a scaffold-only agent.
agent_relevance: Confirms greedy lock-in in a larger study. A scaffold can imitate UCB by computing the bonus outside the model.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan & Griffiths (2023) Cognitive architectures for language agents (CoALA)
finding: Frames LLM agents as production systems with a decision procedure, and notes Soar can use RL to up-weight productions that gave good outcomes. It offers an analogy, not a test of utility-based selection.
numbers: No effect sizes. Mentions the Soar decision cycle (propose, evaluate, select) and RL up-weighting (Nason and Laird 2005).
limits: Conceptual paper. No ACT-R utility experiment.
agent_relevance: Supports putting an explicit select step with learned values between 'propose operators' and 'apply'.
